subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage: Hemant looked at the window. His friends were already playing in the park below. He scribbled the last answers of his maths homework as fast as he could, slammed the notebook shut and ran out. The next day Devika Ma'am returned the books. Two sums had red crosses. "Look at question three, Hemant," she said quietly. He had written 48 where the book said 84, and in the other sum he had left out a zero. He stared at the page. A minute of checking would have caught both, and now he had lost the marks.

qa.q: Which sums did Devika Ma'am mark wrong?
qa.a: She marked two sums wrong, with red crosses.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he saw the two red crosses?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and annoyed with himself. He stared at the page because he knew he could have caught the errors.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Hemant use to check his work quickly, and why?
qa.a: He could read each answer once against the book before closing the notebook. A short check is enough to catch copying slips.

qa.q: How does Devika Ma'am see the two wrong sums?
qa.a: Devika Ma'am sees careless copying errors, not a gap in understanding. That is why she pointed calmly at question three.

grounding: A boy scribbles answers to go out and play and skips checking, so the next day the teacher marks two sums wrong for copying errors.
